summary: This RFC describes using AES in CCM mode within TLS and DTLS to provide confidentiality and data origin authentication. CCM allows compact implementations, which suits constrained environments such as small devices.

eli5.summary: It is a way to scramble and stamp messages that fits on tiny devices, like a lock designed for a very small box.

questions: which tls cipher suites suit constrained devices
what does the _8 in ccm_8 mean
which tls versions can use aes-ccm
how long is the aes-ccm nonce in tls
subtitle: Eight-plus-eight TLS cipher suites that use AES in CCM mode, built for small devices.

tldr.problem: Small, constrained devices need TLS and DTLS cipher suites that encrypt and authenticate data without much code, because CCM needs only the AES encrypt operation.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines 16 cipher suites that use AES-128 or AES-256 in CCM mode as an AEAD algorithm in TLS 1.2, with RSA or pre-shared-key key establishment. Suites ending in _8 use a shorter 8-octet authentication tag instead of 16 octets.
tldr.outcome: They can only be used with TLS 1.2 or later. The RFC is a Proposed Standard, and RFC 10015 updates it.

today: RFC 6655 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 10015. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why AES-CCM in TLS
sections.content:
This RFC describes using the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) in Counter with CBC-MAC mode (CCM) in several TLS cipher suites. CCM gives both confidentiality and authentication, and its only primitive is the AES encrypt operation, so the decrypt operation is not needed. That allows compact implementations, which helps in constrained environments.

The RFC notes that adoption outside such environments is also needed, for example between web clients and embedded servers. It builds on the AEAD facility of TLS 1.2 (RFC 5246) and the AES-CCM algorithms of RFC 5116, and adds AEAD algorithms with shorter authentication tags for networks where bandwidth is constrained and messages are small.
sections.eli5: A small gadget cannot run a big lock. This lock uses just one trick over and over, so it fits in a tiny box.

sections.title: The Cipher Suites
sections.content:
Section 3 defines eight RSA-based suites, with code points {0xC0,0x9C} through {0xC0,0xA3}. They cover RSA and DHE_RSA key exchange, AES-128 and AES-256, and full or _8 tags, for example TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CCM and TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_CCM_8.

Section 4 defines eight pre-shared-key suites, {0xC0,0xA4} through {0xC0,0xAB}, such as TLS_PSK_WITH_AES_128_CCM and TLS_PSK_DHE_WITH_AES_256_CCM_8. PSK and DHE_PSK key exchange follows RFC 4279 and RFC 5487.

Suites ending in _8 have an 8-octet authentication tag; the others have 16-octet tags. All use the default TLS 1.2 pseudorandom function, which uses HMAC with SHA-256. The truncated_hmac extension has no effect on these suites because they do not use HMAC.
sections.eli5: It is a menu of sixteen locks. Some use a shared secret you already have, some use a public key, and some have a shorter seal to save space.

sections.title: The Nonce
sections.content:
The nonce given to the AEAD algorithm is exactly that of RFC 5288. It SHALL be 12 bytes long and is made of a 4-octet salt and an 8-octet nonce_explicit.

The salt is the implicit part and is not sent. It comes from the handshake: client_write_IV when the client sends, server_write_IV when the server sends. The nonce_explicit is chosen by the sender and carried in each TLS record. Each value MUST be distinct for each invocation under a fixed key, and failure to do so can significantly degrade security. It MAY be the 64-bit sequence number. In DTLS the 64-bit value is the 16-bit epoch joined to the 48-bit sequence number.
sections.eli5: Every message needs a number that is never used twice. Part of it is agreed up front, and part travels with each message.

sections.title: Required TLS Versions and the _8 Algorithms
sections.content:
These suites rely on AEAD support, which came with TLS 1.2 and with DTLS version 1.2 (RFC 6347). They MUST NOT be negotiated in older versions. Clients MUST NOT offer them without offering TLS 1.2 or later, and servers that select an earlier version MUST NOT select them. Because a non-compliant server might still pick one with TLS 1.1 or earlier, clients MUST check the version and send a fatal illegal_parameter alert if it is wrong.

Two new AEAD algorithms are defined: AEAD_AES_128_CCM_8 (value 18) and AEAD_AES_256_CCM_8 (value 19). Each is identical to its full-tag counterpart in RFC 5116 except that it uses 8 octets for authentication instead of 16, so the ciphertext is exactly 8 octets longer than the plaintext.
sections.eli5: Older versions of the secret handshake do not know this kind of lock. So nobody may use it with them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC makes two points. First, perfect forward secrecy: only the ephemeral Diffie-Hellman suites (the DHE ones) can provide it. The plain RSA and PSK suites cannot.

Second, AES-CCM security requires that the counter is never reused. The IV construction in the nonce section is designed to prevent counter reuse. The RFC also records that IANA assigned the cipher suite values from the TLS Cipher Suite registry and the AEAD algorithm values from the AEAD Algorithms registry.
sections.eli5: If you want old messages to stay secret even after a key leaks, pick the suites with DHE in the name. And never reuse a number.

fields.name: salt
fields.desc: Implicit part, from client_write_IV or server_write_IV; not sent in the packet.

fields.name: nonce_explicit
fields.desc: Explicit part chosen by the sender and carried in each TLS record; may be the sequence number.
